analysis.one_liner: Requires the Treasury to buy one million Bitcoins and hold them for twenty years.
analysis.headline: The bill to have the U.S. Treasury buy one million Bitcoins has sat in the House Financial Services Committee with no hearing or vote since its March 2025 referral, drawing 10 Republican sponsors and no Democratic support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directs the Treasury Department to buy 200,000 Bitcoins a year for five years — one million total, roughly 5% of all Bitcoin that will ever exist — and hold them in a 'Strategic Bitcoin Reserve' for at least 20 years. The purchases would be paid for by diverting Federal Reserve earnings that would otherwise flow to the Treasury's general fund, cutting the Fed's required surplus, and revaluing the gold certificates held against Treasury gold. After the 20-year lock, the government could sell no more than 10% of the holdings in any two-year period, with proceeds earmarked for reducing the national debt.
analysis.who_benefits: Whoever already owns Bitcoin. A program that buys one million coins — about 5% of the total that can ever exist — directly tightens supply and puts the full faith of the U.S. government behind the asset's price. The cryptocurrency industry gains legitimacy and a permanent federal buyer; the largest holders gain the most, since the run-up in value accrues to coins they already hold.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Existing Bitcoin holders and the crypto industry

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the Treasury to buy 200,000 Bitcoins per year for five years, for a total of one million coins, and to conduct purchases in a way that minimizes market disruption [S3].

All acquired Bitcoin must be held for at least 20 years and cannot be sold, swapped, or encumbered during that period; after it expires, Treasury may not recommend selling more than 10% of the reserve in any two-year period, with sales aimed at reducing the national debt [S3].
The bill builds in transparency: quarterly public cryptographic attestations of holdings verified by an independent third-party auditor, with oversight by the Comptroller General [S3].
It affirms that the government will not seize private Bitcoin holdings and protects individuals' right to self-custody their own coins [S3].
It creates a program letting states voluntarily store their own Bitcoin in segregated federal accounts, retaining title and the right to withdraw [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers and the Treasury's general fund. The purchase money comes from Federal Reserve remittances that would otherwise reduce the deficit, a cut to the Fed banks' required surplus, and an accounting-based revaluation of gold certificates [S3]. The government commits to buying at whatever the market price is — on the order of tens of billions of dollars at 2025 prices — bears all the risk of a notoriously volatile asset, and cannot sell any of it for 20 years no matter what happens to the price.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and the Treasury's general fund

drawbacks.text: The bill obligates the government to buy 200,000 Bitcoins a year for five years regardless of price, exposing taxpayers to a volatile asset with no cost ceiling; at 2025 market prices one million coins would cost on the order of tens of billions of dollars [S3].

The funding is not new revenue: the bill diverts the first $6 billion of Federal Reserve net earnings remitted to the Treasury each year from 2025 through 2029 away from the general fund, and reduces the surplus Federal Reserve banks are allowed to hold from $6.825 billion to $2.4 billion [S3].

The main immediate effect of a government program buying 5% of the total Bitcoin supply is to raise the price of coins held by existing owners; the public upside, if any, arrives only after a 20-year holding period and in limited installments of no more than 10% per two years [S3].

The gold-certificate provision revalues gold held by the Treasury at market price and has the Federal Reserve banks remit the difference, but this is an accounting adjustment between the Fed and the Treasury — it creates a bookkeeping credit, not new real wealth, and critics would note the gold itself does not change [S3].

The Federal government limits its own liability for any loss, theft, or inaccessibility of Bitcoin in the reserve — including state holdings placed there voluntarily — except in cases of gross negligence or willful misconduct [S3].
The purchase program is tied to the Exchange Stabilization Fund, a fund designed for currency intervention, and the bill expands what that fund may hold to include Bitcoin [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to the public are entirely speculative and backloaded: the government cannot sell a single coin for 20 years, and even then only 10% per two-year period, with proceeds going to debt reduction. The costs are near-term and certain — tens of billions in purchases at market price, funded by diverting Federal Reserve remittances that would otherwise shrink the deficit. The design has no price ceiling, no diversification requirement, and the largest guaranteed winners are people who already own Bitcoin before the buying starts. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that this is a bet that Bitcoin keeps rising for two decades, made with public money at whatever price prevails when the buying happens.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Nicholas Begich (R-AK) introduced the BITCOIN Act of 2025 on March 11, 2025, with nine Republican cosponsors joining him at introduction [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction; the complete action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote since [S5].
All ten sponsors and cosponsors are House Republicans; no Democrat has signed on [S4].

The bill would have Treasury buy one million Bitcoins over five years, hold them at least 20 years, and fund purchases through Federal Reserve remittances, a reduced Fed surplus requirement, and revalued gold certificates [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet. Because the bill never moved past referral, taxpayers have not been put on the hook for the purchases; if it stays dormant, the public avoids the price risk and existing Bitcoin holders avoid getting the price boost a government buying program would deliver.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet; the bill has gone nowhere

against.name: French Hill
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill since its referral in March 2025

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors are House Republicans, and no Democrat has signed on; the bill has received no committee action or floor vote that would show broader support.

industries.note: A government program buying one million coins — about 5% of Bitcoin's fixed total supply — would directly push up the price of every coin already in private hands, and the 20-year hold would keep that supply locked up. The largest holders capture that gain immediately, while the public pays the purchase price and bears the volatility risk.

The bill makes the U.S. government a structural, permanent buyer of Bitcoin and puts federal endorsement behind the asset, which would lend the industry legitimacy and a price floor. The industry's gain comes from public purchases whose upside reaches ordinary people only decades later, if at all.

The bill cuts the surplus Fed banks must hold from $6.825 billion to $2.4 billion and diverts the first $6 billion of annual net-earnings remittances to Bitcoin purchases instead of the general fund. The Fed loses remittance capacity, and the Treasury general fund loses money that would otherwise reduce the deficit.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action in the months since referral, no Democratic support, and a first-term sponsor, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing or a floor vote this Congress. A related point: an executive order in March 2025 already directed the federal government to keep forfeited Bitcoin in a 'Strategic Bitcoin Reserve' without buying new coins, so some of the bill's aim is being pursued outside Congress. The bill would likely die in committee unless momentum for federal Bitcoin purchases builds in both chambers.
